items.title: Cheikhou Kouyaté tire sa révérence : « Ô capitaine, mon capitaine ! »
items.description: C'est une page majeure du football sénégalais qui se tourne. Cheikhou Kouyaté, ancien capitaine des Lions et champion d'Afrique en 2022, a annoncé sa retraite ce vendredi. Après plus d'une décennie en équipe nationale, le milieu de terrain laisse l'image d'un cadre fiable, présent dans les grands rendez-vous. « Aujourd’hui, c’est avec beaucoup d’émotion que je vous annonce la fin de ma carrière de footballeur professionnel. Le football a été bien plus qu’un métier. Il a été mon rêve d’enfant, ma passion et le chemin qui m’a permis de devenir l’homme que je suis aujourd’hui. J’ai eu l’honneur de porter les couleurs de grands clubs, de partager le vestiaire avec des joueurs extraordinaires et de défendre mon pays pendant de nombreuses années. Mais ma plus grande fierté restera d’avoir porté le maillot du Sénégal et contribué à écrire une page historique de notre football : la conquête de notre première étoile continentale. Ce jour-là, nous avons offert à tout un peuple de la joie, de l’espoir et un souvenir éternel… ». C'est avec ces mots, publiés sur les réseaux sociaux, que Cheikhou Kouyaté a annoncé avoir raccroché les crampons, à 36 ans. Les chiffres résument à eux seuls une carrière en sélection : 92 sélections et 4 buts, 5 Coupes d'Afrique des nations disputées, deux Coupes du monde (2018 et 2022) et, surtout, un sacre continental en 2022. Le tout dans un parcours marqué, comme le résume l'hommage qui circule ce vendredi, par « l'engagement, l'expérience et le sacre historique du Sénégal à la CAN 2021 ». Il a aussi fait partie de l'épopée des JO 2012 où il s'était révélé avec un certain Sadio Mané… Milieu défensif, parfois utilisé en défense centrale, Kouyaté a toujours été un joueur sur lequel les sélectionneurs pouvaient compter. Il a traversé plusieurs générations de Lions, de la montée en puissance du groupe jusqu'à la consécration. Le sacre de 2022, point d'orgue d'une génération Le titre de champion d'Afrique, remporté lors de la CAN 2021 disputée début 2022 au Cameroun, reste le sommet de son parcours international. Pour le Sénégal, c'était le premier sacre continental de son histoire. Pour Cheikhou Kouyaté, présent dans le groupe depuis des années, c'était la récompense de longues campagnes parfois frustrantes. Il a aussi porté le maillot national lors des Mondiaux 2018 et 2022, deux expériences qui ont installé les Lions parmi les équipes régulières de la scène mondiale. Anderlecht, West Ham, Crystal Palace : un parcours européen solide En club, Kouyaté a construit une belle carrière en Europe. Formé au Sénégal, il a débuté au RSC Anderlecht (2009-2014), où il a décroché quatre titres de champion de Belgique et deux Supercoupes. Il a ensuite rejoint la Premier League, où il a cumulé près de 300 matchs : West Ham United (2014-2018), Crystal Palace (2018-2022), puis Nottingham Forest (2022-2024). Il a terminé par un passage en deuxième division turque, à Amedspor. Cœur et courage Dans une interview à la télévision sénégalaise Walf TV, Kouyaté a révélé vivre depuis sa naissance avec un problème cardiaque. Selon lui, cette condition était suivie de près par les clubs anglais où il a joué, mais elle a aussi compliqué certaines négociations, des clubs hésitant à lui proposer des contrats d'une durée plus longue. Une confidence qui éclaire d'un jour nouveau la longévité d'un joueur ayant évolué au plus haut niveau pendant des années. Ces dernières semaines, Kouyaté était resté proche du groupe, présent dans l'entourage de la sélection pendant le Mondial 2026 sans fonction officielle clairement définie. Sa retraite, jamais annoncée jusque-là, vient désormais clore le chapitre de joueur. Reste à savoir quel rôle il choisira de jouer ensuite dans le football, lui qui avait envisagé de passer à l'encadrement des jeunes. Dans un football où les carrières sont souvent éphémères, Cheikhou Kouyaté aura duré et gagné. Joueur de devoir plus que de lumière, il restera comme l'un des visages de la génération dorée qui a offert au Sénégal sa première CAN. Et maintenant qu’il a tiré sa révérence, dans la discrétion comme le joueur qu’il était, difficile de ne pas penser à ces vers de Walt Whitman dans « Ô Capitaine ! Mon Capitaine ! », où il rendait hommage à Abraham Lincoln après son assassinat le 14 avril 1865 : « Ô Capitaine ! Mon Capitaine ! Lève-toi pour écouter les cloches/ Lève-toi : pour toi le drapeau est hissé, pour toi la trompette sonne (…) ». Certains retiendront peut-être les déclarations maladroites post Coupe du monde, mais ils n’oublieront jamais le joueur de talent, de devoir et de caractère. Le peuple entier chantera sans doute : Merci, Ô Capitaine ! Mon Capitaine ! Oumar Boubacar NDONGO

items.title: Trump calls Nobel Peace Prize pick ‘disgraceful’
items.description: US President Donald Trump slammed the “disgraceful” Nobel Peace Prize choice on Friday as leaving an “indelible stain” on Norway, arguing that the award should have gone to him. South African judge and human rights champion Navi Pillay won the prestigious prize on Friday in recognition of her work against war crimes and crimes against humanity. But Trump labelled the Norwegian Nobel Committee’s choice as “a disgraceful and embarrassing decision”, telling a rally of his supporters in Syracuse, New York he had “never heard of” Pillay. “I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations anyway,” he said. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.” He said the choice of Pillay as laureate left “an indelible stain on the country of Norway”. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the Nobel Peace prize. But his war against Iran, his territorial expansion ambitions as in Greenland, his hard line on migrants, and his attacks on multilateralism and the media disqualified him, according to experts in Oslo speaking before Pillay was announced as laureate. The prize comes with a gold medal, a diploma and a prize sum of $1.2 million. “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation,” Trump said. Pillay had joked about sharing her prize with Trump, telling a crowd who applauded her after the announcement of the award: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” The jibe appeared to be in reference to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who gave her Nobel gold medal to Trump after winning the prize last year. AFP The post Trump calls Nobel Peace Prize pick ‘disgraceful’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Kozah : Le Conseil régional prépare son budget primitif 2027
items.description: Kara, 9 oct. (ATOP) – Le Conseil régional de la Kara a ouvert, le mardi 6 octobre, sa session ordinaire consacrée au bilan des actions réalisées, au suivi des projets d’investissement et à la préparation du budget primitif 2027. Les conseillers régionaux examineront la situation financière de la collectivité arrêtée au 30 septembre 2026, ainsi que l’état d’avancement des projets d’investissement des exercices 2025 et 2026. Ils devront également valider les termes de référence du débat d’orientation budgétaire, préalable à l’élaboration du budget primitif 2027, et étudier les projets structurants à inscrire dans ce budget. Les travaux porteront aussi sur la rencontre tenue à Lomé, les 30 septembre et 1er octobre, avec le directeur de l’Association internationale des régions francophones. Les conseillers prendront par ailleurs connaissance des missions, des réalisations et des perspectives de collaboration de la structure chargée du commerce et de l’industrie au Togo. Le président du Conseil régional, Bakem Teba Blakinam, a présenté les principales réalisations de la collectivité. Il a notamment cité les travaux de construction au Collège d’enseignement technique de Tappé-Ebouya réceptionnés le 1 er septembre dernier pour un montant de 25 millions de FCFA. Il a également évoqué la remise, le 25 septembre, de 200 tables-bancs à quatre établissements secondaires de la préfecture d’Assoli, pour un coût de 9 millions de FCFA. Ces actions visent à améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage des élèves. En matière de développement, le président a annoncé la poursuite des initiatives en faveur de l’accès à l’eau potable au profit des populations bénéficiaires des 18 forages réalisés par le Conseil régional. La collectivité prévoit également d’élaborer son Plan de développement régional afin d’orienter les investissements et les actions à mener au cours des prochaines années. M. Bakem a invité les conseillers à examiner les différents dossiers dans un esprit de responsabilité et de concertation, en tenant compte des besoins des populations de la région. ATOP/AE/AO

items.title: 5 Super Eagles stars who could lose their places in Chelle’s November squad
items.description: Super Eagles head coach Eric Chelle has more selection decisions to make than he did a month ago after the results that surfaced in the just-concluded International break. Nigeria’s 3-0 defeat to Guinea-Bissau exposed several weaknesses, with some established players failing to perform. The result left Nigeria three points behind the Group L leaders and increased the pressure on Chelle ahead of November’s crucial double-header against Tanzania. However, the response against Russia provided a different problem for the coach. Nine players made their Nigeria debuts in the 3-3 draw, while Kelechi Iheanacho, Peter Edokpolor and Abdullahi Bewene were among those who were very impressive. With Nigeria’s next game approaching, Chelle may have to reward hunger and recent performances over reputation, or the stature of some of these players at club level. Super Eagles: 5 players Eric Chelle should drop 1.⁠ ⁠Bright Osayi-Samuel The Birmingham City defender was one of Nigeria’s worst performers in the 3-0 defeat to Guinea-Bissau, after being caught out for both the second and third goals. He was beaten for pace by Mama Baldé before Álvaro Djaló exposed him again in stoppage time. Chelle already has alternatives. Abdullahi Bewene used the Russia friendly to show he belongs with the big boys, providing the assist for Iheanacho’s opener. Ryan Alebiosu has also been in good form for Blackburn Rovers, and will be itching to get a second cap. 2.⁠ ⁠Isaac James James is not yet an established Super Eagles regular, and that is why his performance against Russia could postpone when his second cap comes along. The Alverca defender struggled with some of the basics of the position, despite completing three dribbles, the most of any player in the match. Afrik-Foot rated him 6.2/10 and noted his difficulties knowing when to pass, hold possession and stay back. That means the 22-year-old has not done enough to overtake more experienced names like Bruno Onyemaechi and Zaidu Sanusi. 3.⁠ ⁠Taiwo Awoniyi Awoniyi’s route back into the Super Eagles was created by Osimhen’s injury rather than solid goal-scoring form. He was a late replacement for Osimhen and struggled to make an impression in September. He managed only 22 minutes against Madagascar before starting against Guinea-Bissau and getting withdrawn at half-time after another ineffective display. The problem is what happens when Osimhen returns. If Osimhen and Paul Onuachu are fit, while George Ilenikhena continues scoring in the Saudi Pro League, Awoniyi faces competition from Tolu Arokodare and Kelechi Iheanacho as well, and if he doesn’t outscore them, he’ll most likely not be called up. 4.⁠ ⁠Ademola Lookman Lookman remains one of Nigeria’s most talented players, but his form this season has been poor, scoring just one goal in 10 appearances for club and country across all competitions. Against Madagascar and Guinea-Bissau, the 2024 CAF Player of the Year saw his display characterised by poor first touches, incomplete passes, and half-hearted attempts. There is also new competition arriving behind him. Moses Usor scored on his debut for Nigeria, while Peter Edokpolor scored on his debut against Russia, giving Eric Chelle two new options. Lookman should still be called upon because of his quality, but his starting position should no longer be guaranteed, barring improved form. 5.⁠ ⁠Moses Simon Simon’s case is different. The 31-year-old is a respected senior figure who reached 100 Super Eagles caps during the Madagascar game. However, his importance to the national team is being questioned by his lack of club minutes and end product. Simon has made only four Ligue 1 appearances for Paris FC this season, starting once and playing 133 minutes without a goal or assist. He also struggled to make a decisive impact against Russia. Afrik-Foot rated him 6.7/10 after he failed to turn his runs into anything concrete before being replaced by Edokpolor in the 70th minute. Edokpolor then changed the game. The 19-year-old scored eight minutes after coming on and demonstrated the hunger that Chelle wants from his wingers. That does not erase Simon’s experience and the usefulness of his leadership in the dressing room, but Nigeria do not need to rely on a veteran who is struggling for regular club minutes when younger options are demanding opportunities. Chelle’s November selection dilemma Nigeria cannot afford another poor international break. The Super Eagles are currently three points behind Guinea-Bissau in Group L, while Tanzania are already guaranteed a place at AFCON 2027 as co-hosts. Nigeria need to maximise the November home-and-away meetings against the Taifa Stars. Chelle does not need to discard experience, but the Russia draw showed him that there is a lot of competition for places. For Osayi-Samuel, James, Awoniyi, Lookman and Simon, their club form will determine whether they remain in the starting XI. items.title: Emeka Rollas apologizes to Regina Daniels, mother over comments on marital crisis
items.description: By: Ihemeje Success, Ammah Sarah, Chidinma Nwoobodo & Ojekunle Israel Former President of the Actors Guild of Nigeria, AGN, Emeka Rollas, has apologised to actress Regina Daniels and her mother, Rita Daniels, over comments he made during the actress’s marital crisis with her husband, Senator Ned Nwoko. The clash began in 2025 when Regina and Nwoko’s marital problems became public. Rollas had joined the conversation, making comments about Regina’s well-being and criticising Rita Daniels, suggesting she should focus on her daughter rather than her reported ambition to become AGN president. His remarks angered Regina, who accused him of disrespecting her family. The disagreement later extended to allegations and counter-claims involving AGN leadership and claims about Nwoko’s financial support for the guild. In an apology posted on Instagram, Rollas admitted that he regretted the timing and manner of his comments. He said a recent encounter with Rita Daniels, during an attempt by others to broker peace between them, prompted him to reflect on his actions. “I am human. I made a mistake. I have reflected. And today, I say sincerely: I am sorry,” he stated. “Whether or not anyone chooses to accept my apology is entirely their decision. I am making it because, after looking back, I am not proud of how I handled that moment. “Leadership is not only about having the courage to speak. It is also about having the humility to acknowledge when we could have spoken differently, waited longer, or chosen a better path. “I may still hold my convictions about some of the issues I raised then, but I take responsibility for my actions and my timing,” he added. Regina Daniels, however, responded by questioning Rollas’ apology, accusing him of ingratitude and financial misconduct. items.title: Conakry | Création d’un Conseil d’affaires tuniso-guinéen
items.description: En marge de la mission économique multisectorielle qu’il conduit en en Guinée, du 6 au 11 octobre 2026, le Tunisia Africa Business Council (TABC) a annoncé, le 9 octobre à Conakry, la création du Conseil d’affaires tuniso-guinéen (CATG), destiné à renforcer les échanges commerciaux, les investissements et les partenariats entre les entreprises tunisiennes et guinéennes. Ce lancement marque une nouvelle étape dans le rapprochement des communautés d’affaires des deux pays. Le CATG ambitionne de constituer un cadre permanent de dialogue et de coopération, facilitant l’identification d’opportunités, la mise en relation des opérateurs économiques et le développement de projets conjoints. Le CATG, présidé par Djeneba Keita Hann, compte plusieurs opérateurs économiques guinéens. Du côté tunisien, plusieurs membres de la délégation ont rejoint le CATG. Leur mobilisation permettra de rapprocher les besoins du marché guinéen et les expertises tunisiennes, tout en favorisant des collaborations fondées sur la complémentarité, le transfert de savoir-faire et la création de valeur partagée. Dans un contexte marqué par l’accélération des grands programmes de développement de la Guinée, notamment Simandou 2040, le CATG entend encourager les partenariats dans des secteurs à fort potentiel et développer les investissements des opérateurs économiques Tunisiens en Guinée. À travers des rencontres d’affaires, des missions économiques, des échanges d’informations et un suivi régulier des opportunités identifiées, le CATG ambitionne de donner une continuité concrète aux contacts noués durant cette mission et d’accompagner leur transformation en partenariats durables. items.title: India's 'cockroach' movement chief detained ahead of major protest
items.description: Indian police detained the head of the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement on Saturday ahead of a major protest it called against the Election Commission, the party said. Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital New Delhi, where the demonstration was due to take place, the youth-led CJP said in a social media post. India deployed thousands of police in its capital and restricted transportation in and around Delhi ahead of mass demonstrations on Saturday demanding the resignation of the country’s election chief over alleged voter-roll irregularities. The protests , called by the youth-led CJP , are the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision. Demonstrations erupted across the country after a newspaper investigation last month alleged misconduct by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety in the “special intensive revision”, saying it was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters. Delhi Police personnel stand guard ahead of a protest by the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner over alleged “special intensive revision” (SIR) voter-roll irregularities, near the India Gate in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. — AFP Opposition parties and critics say the exercise could disenfranchise voters to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the usual government-designated protest site. Police have not authorised rallies at the site this weekend. The protests, called by the CJP, are widely seen as a reprise of its mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal. This time, they are demanding ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar resign. ‘Cannot detain the movement’ The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office. Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the Supreme Court on Friday said some trains must still run and that there should be no blanket closure of metro stations. “The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X. “Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.” The CJP, which emerged online as a satirical political movement in May, has accused authorities of intimidating its supporters ahead of the demonstration. The party has said that “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country. Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel stand guard ahead of a protest by the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner over alleged “special intensive revision” (SIR) voter-roll irregularities, in New Delhi on October 10, 2026. — AFP Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported. Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions. “You can detain the people — you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, who has emerged as a leading face of the current protest. The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls. The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died. The poll body said the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots. Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities. Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

items.title: Uche Ogbodo opens up on mistakes, motherhood, building her brand beyond acting
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku Nollywood actress Uche Ogbodo has reflected on her journey in the film industry, describing it as a mix of highs, lows, lessons and resilience. In an interview with us, the mother of three spoke about how she stopped trying to fit into people’s expectations of her and started building her own identity, noting that her lowest moments taught her the most. According to her, playing complicated, villainous and emotionally damaged characters has been the most challenging part of her career because it requires finding humanity in people whose choices differ from hers. On staying relevant in 2026, Ogbodo said talent alone is no longer enough as Nollywood has become more competitive and audiences more sophisticated, adding that she has learned to evolve without losing herself or chasing every trend. The actress also expressed her desire to play a deeply layered, emotionally raw role that shows vulnerability beyond beauty and strength — a woman whose life looks perfect outside but is different behind closed doors. On balancing acting, business and motherhood, Ogbodo admitted that she doesn’t always have it together but has learned to prioritize, delegate, say no and protect her energy. She described her personal brand as reinvention, courage, femininity and resilience, stressing that she has refused to be defined by one chapter of her life. Addressing misconceptions about her, the actress said while many see her as tough and unbothered, she is actually very sensitive and feels deeply, but has learned to survive her emotions without allowing them to destroy her. You have come a long way in Nollywood. When you look back, how would you describe your journey so far? My journey has been a beautiful mix of highs, lows, lessons, reinvention and resilience. I started as a young girl with a dream, and today I’m a woman who has lived through so many different chapters. My biggest turning point was learning to understand who I am outside of what people expect me to be. I stopped trying to fit into people’s idea of Uche Ogbodo and started building my own identity. My lowest moments taught me the most. There were periods when I felt broken, disappointed and completely exhausted, but somehow I always found a reason to get back up. I think that’s one thing about me, I may bend, but I don’t stay down. You’ve played a wide range of characters—the strong woman, the lover, the villain. Which role challenged you the most? The roles that challenge me most are the ones that require me to become someone completely different from Uche Ogbodo. I love playing complicated women because real women are complicated. The villainous or emotionally damaged characters can be particularly challenging because you have to find humanity in someone whose choices may be completely different from yours. That’s where the real acting happens. Nollywood has changed a lot. How have you evolved as an actress to stay relevant in 2026? I’ve learned that talent alone isn’t enough anymore. You have to evolve. The industry has become more competitive, audiences are more sophisticated, and social media has completely changed how actors connect with people. I’ve had to reinvent myself, understand my audience and remain open to new ways of telling stories. But I’ve also learned not to chase every trend. Relevance is knowing how to evolve without losing yourself. What’s one script or story you’ve always wanted to play but haven’t got the chance yet? I’d love to play a deeply layered woman whose life looks perfect from the outside but is completely different behind closed doors—a woman navigating love, motherhood, ambition, sexuality, betrayal, power and reinvention. Something emotionally raw. Something that makes people uncomfortable, laugh, cry and think. I want a role that doesn’t just show me as beautiful or strong. I want to show vulnerability. You’re very open about motherhood. How has being a mom changed the way you choose roles and run your career? Motherhood has made me much more intentional. Before, I could make decisions purely based on ambition. Now, I have people whose lives are connected to mine, so I think about my time, my values and the kind of example I’m setting. But being a mother hasn’t made me stop being a woman with dreams. If anything, it has made me more ambitious because I want my children to see a woman who didn’t abandon herself while raising them. You balance acting, business and raising kids. What’s your secret to staying sane and organized? I don’t always have it together! I’ve learned to prioritize. Everything cannot be urgent, and everything doesn’t deserve my energy. I delegate where I can, I plan my time, and I’ve become much better at saying no. And sometimes, I simply disappear and recharge. You cannot pour from an empty cup. I’ve learned that protecting my energy is not selfish. You’ve built a strong personal brand on and off screen. What does “Uche Ogbodo” represent to you? Uche Ogbodo represents reinvention, courage, femininity and resilience. I’m a woman who has refused to be defined by one chapter of her life. I’m an actress, I’m a mother, I’m a businesswoman, I’m a woman who loves fashion and beauty, and I’m also somebody who has made mistakes and learned from them. My brand is really about being unapologetically myself. What’s the biggest lesson life has taught you in the last five years? You cannot live your life trying to please everybody. People will judge you whether you do right or wrong. They’ll love you today and criticize you tomorrow. So I’ve learned to live according to my values, protect my peace and make decisions that I can live with. Life is too short to constantly perform for other people. What’s a misconception people have about you that you’d love to correct? People sometimes think I’m this extremely tough, confident woman who doesn’t care what anybody thinks. The truth is, I’m actually very sensitive. I feel deeply, I love deeply. Things affect me. I just learned how to survive my emotions without allowing them to destroy me. And yes, I’m confident—but confidence doesn’t mean I don’t have vulnerable moments. I think people sometimes mistake my strength for not having feelings. I have feelings. I just refuse to let them stop me from living. The post Uche Ogbodo opens up on mistakes, motherhood, building her brand beyond acting appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘Tinubu has removed the corruption’ — Oyedele faults Obi’s subsidy plan
items.description: The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has faulted the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, Peter Obi’s proposal to restore petrol subsidy if elected, arguing that President Bola Tinubu’s removal of the subsidy has already addressed the corruption associated with the system. Oyedele stated this during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today , where he defended and justified the Federal Government’s 30-day petrol price discount. Obi had recently pledged to restore petrol subsidy after tackling corruption if elected president in 2027. However, Oyedele questioned the logic of the proposal, arguing that restoring subsidy would risk reintroducing the same problems the current administration sought to eliminate. “With what Mr President has done, he has removed the corruption. So would you bring the corruption back so that you can fight it, remove it, and then bring back subsidy? It’s not adding up,” the minister said. Oyedele also dismissed suggestions that petrol prices could be substantially reduced to between N400 and N1,000 per litre without addressing the underlying costs of production and refining. “You cannot cut the price of petrol to N400, not N500, not N800, not N1000. It’s simple arithmetic. What are the inputs?” he asked. He explained that refining was a low-margin business that depended largely on high production volumes, making it difficult for operators to sustain significant price reductions without a corresponding reduction in costs. Responding to a question about why crude oil produced in Nigeria could not be supplied to domestic refiners at lower prices, Oyedele said crude oil production involved several costs and contractual obligations. He noted that crude oil revenue was shared among production costs, international oil companies, royalties and profit oil, meaning that the country could not treat all its output as freely available for domestic use. “The fact that you have 1.8 million barrels plus constantly condensate a day does not mean that all of it is available for you to give to anyone,” he said. The minister warned that selling crude oil below market prices to support cheaper petrol would reduce government revenue and potentially affect its ability to meet obligations, including salary payments. He also argued that maintaining artificially low domestic fuel prices could encourage cross-border smuggling and distort the market. According to Oyedele, Nigeria’s petrol consumption had previously approached 90 million litres daily, but not all the fuel was consumed within the country. He cited protests in Cameroon following Tinubu’s removal of petrol subsidy as an indication of how differences in fuel prices could affect neighbouring countries. Oyedele further argued that even the United States had not been able to secure its borders completely, questioning the feasibility of relying on border enforcement alone to prevent the diversion of subsidised petrol. items.title: ‘Betrayal of international law’: US sanctions on ICC draw widespread condemnation
items.description: US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the ​International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize , putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order” and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. “The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC said in a statement, adding that the issue was about safeguarding the international order grounded in the rule of law. “The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes,” it said. The move drew widespread condemnation from governments, human rights activists and international organisations, including the United Nations. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the US announcement of sanctions against the ICC as an institution. In a statement, he said “accountability for international crimes and the delivery of justice to victims were central to the global commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms”. UN Guterres reiterated his unwavering support for the independence of the court and its officials. The foreign ministry of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement opposing the sanctions. “As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States,” the statement said, as shared by Germany’s Foreign Office on X. The ministers also welcomed the court’s preparations to ensure it could continue to fulfil its mandate under the Rome Statute, reaffirming their support for its work. Japan also issued a statement backing the court, joining the other countries in opposing the US move and reiterating its support for the ICC’s ability to carry out its mandate. Belgium condemned the sanctions, saying “the ICC must be able to operate independently”. It called for the activation of the European Union’s Blocking Statute to protect the court. Human rights advocates warned that the sanctions threatened justice for victims of abuses in Palestine, Ukraine, Myanmar and Sudan, describing the move as “an unprecedented assault on global justice and the rule of law”. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the ICC as the “cornerstone of the international criminal justice system”. She said she had spoken with ICC President Tomoko Akane following Washington’s announcement, adding that the six-month period before the sanctions take effect offered an opportunity for dialogue. “The EU has always supported the Court, and the EU has options to ensure that it can continue its vital work,” Kallas said, adding that protecting the ICC remained an EU priority. The United Kingdom’s Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs also condemned the sanctions in a post on X, saying: “The UK stands with the International Criminal Court and we stand united with our partners in strongly disagreeing with sanctions imposed on the Court. “The ICC must be permitted to continue its critical work holding perpetrators of the most horrific international crimes to account.” Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard criticised the sanctions, describing the move as “a betrayal” of the principles of international criminal law. In a post on X, she urged European governments to “impose immediately blocking orders” to prevent the sanctions from being implemented on European territory. The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met. Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and ​an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is “deprioritised.

items.title: Le Maroc offre une vitrine à l’armement israélien en pleine guerre à Gaza
items.description: Malgré l’hostilité d’une bonne partie de son opinion publique, le Maroc continue de renforcer ses relations avec Israël, dont l’entreprise génocidaire à Gaza et le nettoyage ethnique en Cisjordanie occupée suscitent de plus en plus le désaveu, y compris parmi ses soutiens traditionnels en Occident. Alors que les portes lui sont fermées aux salons de Paris et de Rotterdam, l’industrie de défense israélienne se voit offrir une vitrine par le royaume du Maroc. Israël expose pour la première fois ses armes au Maroc En effet, pour la première fois, des entreprises de défense israéliennes participent officiellement au Salon aéronautique de Marrakech, qui se tient du 7 au 10 octobre. Conduite par la Direction de la coopération internationale en matière de défense du ministère israélien de la Défense, connue sous l’acronyme SIBAT, la délégation israélienne comprend huit entreprises : Elbit Systems, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, XTEND Systems, SHILAT Optronics, UVision Air, ASIO Technologies et Orbit Communication Systems, selon les comptes rendus de plusieurs médias. Les équipements présentés couvrent plusieurs domaines : munitions téléopérées, systèmes robotiques fondés sur l’intelligence artificielle, navigation autonome pour drones, guidage laser de drones FPV et communications satellitaires. Elbit Systems expose notamment le drone Hermes 900, des plateformes autonomes de la famille FUSE, ainsi que la munition rôdeuse SkyStriker, le système de lance-roquettes PULS et le projectile guidé par laser LIZARD. De son côté, Israel Aerospace Industries met en avant des technologies de frappe de précision et des systèmes de défense, dont le missile LORA. Les trois grands groupes présentent plus largement des solutions destinées aux domaines aérien, terrestre, naval et spatial, ainsi qu’au renseignement et au cyberespace. Génocide à Gaza et nettoyage ethnique en Cisjordanie Cette présence, qui intervient dans un contexte international sensible, marqué notamment par la persistance des violences israéliennes contre les Palestiniens, ne passe pas inaperçue. Car les industriels israéliens exposent des technologies militaires qu’ils présentent eux-mêmes comme « éprouvées au combat » à Gaza, notamment des drones, des munitions rôdeuses, des systèmes de guidage et des équipements de communication. Autrement dit, des technologies dont la valeur commerciale est également mise en avant à travers leur utilisation opérationnelle sur les théâtres de guerre. Et qui dit théâtres de guerre dit opérations menées par l’entité sioniste en Iran, au Liban et en Syrie, mais surtout dans l’enclave de Gaza, martyrisée et dévastée. À Marrakech, les responsables israéliens ne boudent d'ailleurs pas leur plaisir face à cette opportunité et ne cachent pas les objectifs de cette participation. Le général de brigade à la retraite Yaïr Kulas, qui dirige la SIBAT, a lui-même qualifié cette présence de « jalon important » pour le ministère de la Défense et l’industrie militaire israélienne, selon les mêmes sources. Il a également présenté le salon comme une plateforme destinée à « élargir la coopération internationale en matière de défense et à établir des partenariats à long terme ». Derrière la vitrine technologique se dessine donc un objectif commercial, mais surtout stratégique : accroître les exportations d’armements israéliens, prospecter de nouveaux marchés et consolider les liens militaires avec Rabat. Pour le Royaume, engagé dans une course à l’armement, cette participation, qui s’inscrit dans le prolongement des accords d’Abraham, constitue une occasion de renforcer davantage ses liens avec Israël. Une coopération à contre-courant de l’opinion publique Mais au moment où, en Occident, des gouvernements durcissent le ton à l’égard d’Israël et où les entreprises israéliennes rencontrent des restrictions dans certains grands salons européens de défense, la participation israélienne au salon de Marrakech dans ce contexte particulier apparaît comme un affront à l’opinion publique marocaine et aux Palestiniens. D’autant que cette présence coïncide avec l’anniversaire du 7 octobre, date de l’attaque du Hamas en Israël, en 2023, qui a déclenché la guerre à Gaza et les opérations militaires israéliennes ayant entraîné des pertes humaines massives et des destructions considérables dans le territoire palestinien. Une coïncidence qui confère à cette participation une dimension politique supplémentaire. Mais qu’importe, visiblement, pour les autorités marocaines. L’enjeu est ailleurs : il se situe avant tout sur le terrain stratégique et industriel. Le rapprochement avec Israël lui permet de bénéficier de technologies avancées et de renforcer ses capacités militaires face à son voisin algérien. De quoi entretenir l'instabilité dans une région qui ne manque pas de foyers de tensions. L’article Le Maroc offre une vitrine à l’armement israélien en pleine guerre à Gaza est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: R. Stahl ouvre un bureau à Tunis
items.description: R. Stahl, groupe spécialisé dans la protection antidéflagrante, ouvre son bureau tunisien à l'IQ Smart Building & Business Center, Boulevard Qualité de la Vie, Le Kram, Tunis. Le bureau sera inauguré au cours ‘une cérémonie officielle le lundi 12 octobre 2026, de 17h à 19h, en présence de Tobias Popp, vice-président et directeur commercial du groupe qui compte des filiales dans 20 pays. L’évènement sera marqué par la signature d'un accord d'adhésion entre R. Stahl et la Chambre tuniso-allemande de l’industrie et du commerce (AHK Tunisie). R. Stahl assure une distribution mondiale et la conduite de projets internationaux sur plusieurs continents. Avec cette implantation en Tunisie, le groupe entend structurer un pôle de développement logiciel, destiné à accélérer le déploiement de ses solutions en mode Software-as-a-Service (SaaS). Dans un second temps, le site a vocation à évoluer en Centre de Services Partagés (CSP). Le chiffre d’affaires consolidé de R. Stahl AG pour l’exercice 2025 s’est élevé à 313,0 millions d'euros (dont 71,5 M€ en Allemagne), en baisse de 9,1 % par rapport à l’exercice 2024 (où il atteignait 344,1 millions d’euros). La protection antidéflagrante (souvent désignée sous le marquage Ex d ou Ex db) est une méthode de sécurité qui consiste à enfermer les composants risquant de provoquer une explosion à l’intérieur d'un boîtier ultra-résistant. items.title: Let The Constitution direct Chieftaincy to deliver “All Development Is Local”
items.description: By Kwasi Ansu-Kyeremeh, The Chieftaincy Institute Chieftaincy’s natural power and capacity to lead local development have been grossly underrated and it is time to address that constitutionally. For accelerated local development, there is an urgent need to reverse the constitutional usurpation of that local development role which it assigns to local government. Article 245(a) of Ghana’s 1992 Constitution mandates a decentralised system of local government and administration to drive local development. So far, the article has underperformed in implementation, such that the Constitution Review Committee (CRC) seeks its review in an “all development is local” approach. To fix the local development deficit, CRC recommends “introduce direct elections for local government chief executives (MMDCEs),” instead of currently being appointed; together with the establishment of an Independent Devolution Commission (IDC) to intensify decentralisation and invigorate local development authority. That sets a task for the Constitution Review Implementation Committee (CRIC) to enact constitutional intervention to remedy the little development at the local level which tends to slow national development. For that transformative local governance for accelerated local development, chieftaincy (as in occupiers of skins and stools), stands ready for consideration by CRIC as the logical apparatus. Even so, item 12 (electing MMDCEs) of the 13 points of action by CRIC seems far less capable of addressing that task of an article of local empowerment for local development as “fapem” (bedrock) of national development Yet, dare one mention chieftaincy as the more viable agency for accelerated local development, and an initial reaction will likely be that it is too dividing and less uniting over succession issues to champion development. Fact, though, is that the negative of chieftaincy as source of conflict is overblown, while the institution’s massive potential as agent for local development, is woefully underrated. A constitution is made to last, but it must first tackle the now issues. They say “72% of Ghanaian youth have considered leaving the country” for lack of employment opportunity. Tertiary students and graduates are actively involved in galamsey. The National Development Planning Commission (NDPC) attributes the syndrome of abandoned projects to “political discontinuity” and “lack of legal enforcement.” And despite legislation, public procurement abuse is widespread. As macro issues that they might be, they have implications for local development. Historically, though, Biadanhene (chief) Nana Kwasi Ansu in the Berekum Traditional Area led his people to provide themselves with real development. Within two short years in the 1950s, the chiefdom provided itself with pipe-borne water and a community centre with day nursery annexed building complex. A farm trail was upgraded to a motorable road; and a generating plant was procured to supply electricity. Such micro activity can serve as the foundation for national development. These days, from the village head (adikrofoɔ) through subchiefs (abrempɔn) to paramount chiefs (amanhene) all the way to the Asantehene, chiefs are still able to utilise their paltry traditionally decentralised authority to develop their areas. They mobilise to provide health and education facilities, social amenities and infrastructure to stimulate economic activity for the development of their chiefdoms. Just imagine what chieftaincy can do with its authority boosted by the constitution. Basically, chieftaincy is “democratic government to a degree of which there is not any modern parallel in Europe,” with decentralisation as “one of its outstanding characteristics.” It is centripetally bottom-up and, therefore, naturally sensitive to local development. Chieftaincy democracy develops where “election democracy” may not. Thus, the institution deserves the restoration of its authority to develop which is constitutionally usurped in local government with the 1992 Constitution. At each level of the chieftaincy hierarchy, the leader/chief is sufficiently empowered and reseanobly resourced with the autonomy and power to mobilise at each level of the hierarchy to develop the jurisdiction/chiefdom; no dependence on the centre to decentralise/devolve/disburse authority or resources before initiating, planning and implementing local development. Traditional leaders are more knowledgeable, have richer lived life experiences and, by that, better prepared as development leaders than the political class. The former are empowered and compelled by culture, tradition and customary practice to mobilise human and material (land) resources to improve the living conditions of their people. And the institution’s gender inclusive queenmother role strengthens the active participation of women in the thinking and doing of local development that leads to national development. Among the tools available to the chief for the mobilisation and execution of a local development agenda are the network of vertical sub-authorities in subchiefs, courtiers and other chiefly actors and the horizontal abusua (family/clan) groups with defined heads. A chief also has the power to create nkɔsoɔ (development) and boafoɔ (helper) stool occupants to specifically spearhead development activity. Also at his disposal are devices such as the dawuro concept for effective communication. Some skins and stools own communication centres, radio stations, websites or are robustly present on various social media platforms. Alternatively, whatever its strengths, the imported local government, as is practised now by Chapter 20 of the 1992 Constitution, is severely limited productively, satisfactorily and effectively as a replacement for chieftaincy in promoting development at the grassroots. Decentralised authority for the local to develop itself within the broader national context is endlessly pursued or it “has collapsed;” or “dysfunctional.” Others think it is “centralisation of decentralistion;” that the central government develops the underdevelopment of the local area. With its built-in politics of ampɛbrɛ (shuns hard work), ammɔbra (unachieved), kakistocratic and kleptocratic tendencies, local government political actors are engaged in some kind of operation hide the loot, employing all schemes to evade asset tracking and lifestyle audit accountability. Indeed, chieftaincy’s organic dynamics surpasses the superficial workings of local government in linking the people to their life struggles. What is missing in a development transformative role for chieftaincy is the constitutional mandate to develop as assigned to local governemnent in Article 245(a)(b) of the 1992 Constitution. With chieftaincy, if there are lapses in development thought and action, it is possibly due to development being voluntary and not being required by law. A constitutionally reorganised Chief-in-Council (CiC) local governance system that incorporates the tappable elements of both chieftaincy and local government. It inherits chieftaincy’s already effectively decentralised structure and quality leadership that thinks and does great local development. A lead chief (rotational among peers) would preside over a council of elected and appointed on merit membership. Term limits are to be enforced and where there is only one senior chief, the next (set) in grade shall be promoted to occupy the position (by rotation). Structurally, the CiC has the features of: 1) merged authority 2) enhanced resourcing 3) guaranteed tenure and, therefore, continuity of programmes and projects post-election changes, 4) accountability and transparency 5) effective monitoring and supervision 6) quality leadership in a combination of knowledge and lived life experience, not ampɛbrɛ and ammɔbra political appointees and 7) prospects for rapid industrialisation. It is proposed for the consideration of the CRIC, that the CiC organ will be the constitutional replacement for the current dualised paralleling local governance system of chieftaincy and local government. Its structure also incorporates advisory committees which might co-opt outside expertise to enhance decision-making and implementation. A specialised standing committee on women and associated issues, is to be chaired by the queenmother. Committees will deliberate the affairs of the units for in-depth knowledge to guide policy formulation and implementation. An administrator, appointed on merit, will run a bureaucracy organised into functional units. Each unit is to be headed by a person with technical knowledge of the area. Among unit responsibilities are to research, offer technical advice and help implement programmes and projects. One envisages enhanced opportunity of increased economic activity with the chief in charge to push for rapid industrialisation and development of the people in local communities. With a key focus on job creation, the chief-led CiC may want to explore clues and cues from Nkrumah’s cottage industries, Busia’s rural industries, Kufuor’s presidential initiatives and Akufo-Addo’s one village one dam/one district one factory as they affected local industrialisation. CONCLUSION It is time the Constitution took advantage of our own indigenous institutions to define and pursue our common development destiny by constitutionally redirecting the effort and resources for improving the local government system towards strengthening the empowerment of the chieftaincy institution to deliver “all development is local,” especially by strengthening its leadership accountability mechanisms. For a meaningful impact on the lives of ordinary Ghanaians, any change in the constitution regarding local development must necessarily begin with the recognition of chieftaincy as the primary local development agency. It is the people, with leadership of occupants of skins and stools who combine sukuu nyansa (knowledge) and efie nyansa (wisdom) with rich life experiences. That makes the traditional leader better prepared for executing the local development task than the transient political actors of less connection to the people and less so equipped to lead to develop. Chieftaincy is unable to vigorously pursue its development responsibility because the authority to do so is usurped by the constitutional local government. Presently, lapses in development thought and action partly because the chief’s development responsibility not mandatory but rather voluntary. Chieftaincy must be treated as transformable, constitutionally formulated as transformative development apparatus for the aggressive pursuit of an “all development is local” agenda. That must be the focus and product of a CRIC organised 12 th of the13 points of constitutional review. Otherwise, the huge costs of the review of the 1992 Constitution since 2010 would have effectively betrayed the people and failed the CRC’s cardinal recommendation of local development for, and as, national development. Lest we forget the grassroots chant the authors/originators of the 1992 Constitution have forgotten by grabbing USD1.7 billion gold heist: “Ghana people we are always fighting for our rights. We no go sit down make dɛm cheat us every day. Daabi da!!!” Just imagine a constitution that mandates chiefs as the main agency for the development of their chiefdoms. It will no longer be “their” intervention project or programme but us empowered to develop of us, for us, in us, by us, about us, and to us!!!

items.title: Trump sows doubt on plan to livestream US military execution
items.description: US President Donald Trump has cast doubt on whether authorities will livestream the firing squad execution of the perpetrator of a deadly attack on American soldiers, a plan that has drawn broad and bipartisan condemnation , it emerged on Saturday. Nidal Hasan’s execution — scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 — is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945. A Pentagon official told AFP on Thursday that the execution would be streamed live, after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” But Trump, who supports the death penalty in this case, left it uncertain whether the execution would be publicly broadcast. “They are making a determination about that, but he will be killed,” Trump said. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes.” Earlier Friday, Vice President JD Vance told journalists who asked about the planned livestream that he does not “know that that’s actually going to happen.” “This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Vance said, but added that if the execution is broadcast live, “I’m not going to be watching it.” Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice” but that public executions are “the kind of thing Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?” Tech firms YouTube, Meta and X did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether they would allow the execution to be streamed on their platforms. TikTok directed AFP to its policy banning depictions of “graphic incidents and violence” including “the shooting of an individual.” The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights condemned the plan, saying in a message sent to AFP on Friday that “the livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture.” Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.” ‘Compound the cruelty’ Hegseth said it would be the military’s first firing squad execution since World War II. “People need to understand that… there’s serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth said in a video shared Thursday on official Pentagon X accounts. The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder. The Death Penalty Information Centre says 135 troops have been executed by the US military since 1916. According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 — six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran. Amnesty’s Justin Mazzola said Friday that the death penalty is “a violation of human rights,” and that streaming Hasan’s execution “would only compound the cruelty.” Twelve of the 13 people Hasan killed and 30 of those he wounded were soldiers. He was shot by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack and is paralysed from the waist down. Hasan chose to conduct his own defence during the trial but called no witnesses and gave no testimony, and made no attempt to deny the charges. He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013. Court-appointed defence attorneys expressed concern that he was seeking execution. The court that convicted Hasan was told he was opposed to the US military’s occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.

items.title: 2027: What insecurity may do to APC’s bid
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The road to an NYSC orientation camp became a kidnapping route on October 1 when gunmen attacked buses near Umunoha in Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State and abducted prospective corps members. Six days later, 20 of them were rescued. Read Also: 2027: 30 days can’t erase over three years of hardship, Atiku tells Tinubu They were young Nigerians travelling for a national service programme. Their ordeal carried a political question far bigger than the incident itself: how safe are Nigerians on the roads they must use? That question is beginning to sit alongside the economy, cost of living and governance in calculations for 2027. For President Bola Tinubu, insecurity is not yet an electoral verdict, but it is becoming a vulnerability the administration cannot afford to ignore. The road to 2027 runs through security Nigerians do not experience insecurity through statistics. They experience it when children leave for school, farmers head to their fields, traders travel, worshippers return home or families wait for abducted relatives. The Imo incident carried significance beyond another kidnapping. It involved young Nigerians on a journey meant to symbolise national integration, yet their route became a site of fear and criminal control. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) says mass kidnappings averaged at least 100 incidents per quarter in 2025, compared with fewer than 70 per quarter in 2026 so far. The level is lower than last year’s peak, but still elevated. ACLED also says armed bandits accounted for more than 80 per cent of recorded mass abductions since early 2025, with ransom increasingly important to financing such violence. That leaves Tinubu facing a political test: can increased security spending and operations translate into a visible improvement in the everyday sense of safety? Rescue is not the same as prevention The administration has a substantial record of security interventions. It declared a nationwide security emergency in 2025, expanded recruitment, redeployed some police officers from VIP protection, backed forest guards and surveillance, and pushed intelligence-led operations and military modernisation. The 2026 budget proposed N5.41 trillion for defence and security. Finding a kidnappers’ camp is not the same as preventing an abduction. Rescuing hostages is not the same as arresting abductors. Arresting suspects is not the same as dismantling the networks, financiers, informants and routes that make another attack possible. The Imo episode raises operational questions. How did the attackers identify and stop the buses? Was the route regarded as vulnerable? Were intelligence agencies sharing information before the attack? How quickly could security forces move after the camp was located? Human rights lawyer and activist, Deji Adeyanju, told Saturday Vanguard in Abuja that insecurity could become a serious political challenge for Tinubu because its consequences are deeply personal for Nigerians. “Insecurity is not simply a question of statistics or the number of attacks recorded,” Adeyanju Opposition sees an opening Mark Adebayo, Head of the Directorate of Media and Communications of the Adewole Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign, said the crisis had serious implications for Tinubu’s re-election prospects and the legitimacy of the state. “The political implications of Nigeria’s worsening security situation ahead of the 2027 general elections are profound, primarily threatening President Bola Tinubu’s reelection bid and undermining state legitimacy,” Adebayo told Saturday Vanguard. He attributed the administration’s difficulties to what he described as uncoordinated counter-terrorism strategies, alleged military corruption and a perceived disconnect from grassroots realities. Those are opposition arguments, and some wider performance and casualty claims require verification. Politically, however, the opposition needs to persuade voters that the government has not made them safer. The voters will have the final say Insecurity will not automatically deliver votes to the opposition. Its political effect could be subtler: punishment of the incumbent, declining confidence, or reduced turnout where voters fear violence. A Yiaga Africa survey found that 84 per cent of respondents were willing or likely to vote, but 61 per cent said fear of violence could prevent them from doing so. In the North-East, the figure rose to 78 per cent. Security also ranked among the leading issues respondents wanted addressed. Voters may punish a government they believe has failed to protect them. But insecurity may also suppress turnout without transferring those votes to an opponent. The regional picture matters. In the North-East, insurgency and election-related violence remain major concerns. In the North-West, banditry and mass kidnapping dominate the security conversation. The North-Central faces attacks on farming communities and displacement, while parts of the South-East and South-South contend with road kidnapping, separatist violence and criminal networks. For insecurity to become a decisive electoral liability, several developments may have to converge: continued high-profile abductions despite increased spending; attacks spreading into previously safer areas; slow or contradictory official responses; repeated rescues without arrests or prosecutions; continuing ransom payments; and a growing connection between insecurity, food prices and economic hardship. Anger is not an electoral strategy. The opposition must convince voters that it can do better, finance security, improve intelligence coordination, protect highways and bring perpetrators to justice. Tinubu still has time to change the argument. A sustained decline in attacks, safer highways, disruption of kidnapping finances, prosecutions and faster responses would give the administration something more powerful than another security announcement: evidence. The political verdict will not be determined by budgets or troop numbers alone. It will depend on whether Nigerians see measurable improvements in their security before they cast their ballots. For Tinubu, the challenge is therefore clear: turn security operations into safer roads, fewer abductions and greater confidence that the state can protect its citizens. If that happens, insecurity may remain a difficult issue without becoming a decisive electoral liability. If it does not, the opposition will have a ready-made case against the administration in 2027. Vanguard News The post 2027: What insecurity may do to APC’s bid appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: John Jinapor outlines renewable energy, nuclear power priorities for 2027
items.description: The Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, has outlined plans to accelerate Ghana’s transition towards cleaner and more sustainable energy, identifying renewable energy expansion, mini-grid projects and the advancement of the Ghana Nuclear Power Programme as key priorities for 2027. He said the government remained committed to diversifying the country’s energy mix, expanding electricity access and strengthening the resilience of the national power system to meet the country’s growing energy needs. Addressing the 2026 Energy Sector Performance Review Retreat, Dr Jinapor said the Ministry and its agencies must move beyond planning and focus on delivering measurable results in the coming year. “As we look towards 2027, therefore, our focus must be clear: from plans to implementation; from commitments to measurable results; and from promises to delivery,” he stated. The minister identified the expansion of solar and other renewable energy projects, completion of 35 mini-grids, expansion of solar home systems and net-metering, and promotion of clean cooking initiatives as priority areas requiring accelerated implementation. He also stressed the importance of advancing the Ghana Nuclear Power Programme as part of efforts to establish a more diversified and sustainable energy system. According to Dr Jinapor, renewable energy capacity had increased to 345 megawatts, while the country’s installed electricity generation capacity stood at 5,854MW. Electricity access had also risen to 89.13 per cent. He said these developments demonstrated progress in expanding the country’s energy infrastructure but noted that more work was required to ensure reliable electricity supply and improve access across the country. The minister emphasised that the transition to cleaner energy must go hand in hand with investments in generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure to ensure that electricity could be delivered efficiently to homes, businesses and industries. He also called for stronger institutional coordination and accountability, insisting that agencies must clearly define their targets, resource requirements and implementation timelines for 2027. “Every Agency must clearly state what it achieved in 2026, what it intends to achieve in 2027, the resources required, and the timelines for delivery,” he said. Dr Jinapor further urged the agencies to ensure that all projects were implemented in accordance with procurement laws and regulations, stressing that the pursuit of faster delivery must not undermine transparency, accountability or value for money. He said the government’s energy agenda was aimed at building a system that could withstand external shocks while supporting industrial development and economic growth. “Above all, let us deliver an energy sector that is reliable, affordable, sustainable and resilient, and that supports the economic transformation of Ghana,” he stated. The 2026 Energy Sector Performance Review Retreat is expected to provide a platform for the Ministry and its agencies to assess their performance during the year, review outstanding commitments and agree on measurable targets and priorities for 2027.

items.title: Rapport de HRW sur l'Ouganda: les États-Unis se servent de l'accord pour annuler les demandes d'asile
items.description: Depuis janvier 2025, les États-Unis ont annulé plus de 2 700 procédures d’asile sans même examiner les demandes sur le fond. Le motif : ces personnes - pour la plupart africaines - pourraient solliciter une protection en Ouganda, en vertu d’un accord conclu en juillet 2025 entre Washington et Kampala. C’est l’une des conséquences de la politique d’expulsions vers des pays africains mise en place par l’administration Trump, et dénoncée dans un rapport de Human Rights Watch publié le 8 octobre. Pour Michael Garcia Bochenek, l’un des auteurs de ce rapport, il s’agit tout simplement d’un contournement du droit d’asile américain.

items.title: UNILAG Faculty mourns Sobowale, celebrates legacy
items.description: The Faculty of Communication and Media Studies, University of Lagos (UNILAG), has mourned the passing of Professor Idowu Akanbi Sobowale, OON, a distinguished scholar, veteran journalist, astute administrator who died on October 8, 2026 at the age of 85. In a statement by the Dean of the Faculty, Professor Oloruntola Sunday, he described Professor Sobowale, a former student, lecturer and Head of department of Mass Communication in UNILAG, as one of the foremost pioneers of Mass Communication education and practice in Nigeria. According to Professor Sunday, Professor Sobowale was “a professor of professors, whose intellectual depth, commitment to academic excellence and dedication to mentorship helped shape the careers of numerous students and colleagues.” The Dean noted that through Sobowale’s guidance and encouragement, many of those he mentored went on to distinguish themselves across diverse fields of endeavour, extending his influence far beyond the classroom and the institutions he served. He recalled that the late university don pioneered the introduction of scientific public opinion polling to Nigerian journalism. This, he said, remains one of his most enduring contributions to the communication profession. “Through his work with The Punch newspaper, he helped establish a foundation for the systematic study of public opinion in Nigeria, advancing evidence-based journalism and enriching public discourse,” he said. “His commitment to research demonstrated the power of scholarship to inform professional practice and contribute meaningfully to society.” Professor Sobowale’s passing according to the Dean, represents a profound loss to the University of Lagos, the Nigerian academic community and the global communication fraternity. The Faculty stated that Professor Sobowale’s intellectual contributions, professional accomplishments and enduring commitment to the advancement of Mass Communication will remain an invaluable part of the discipline’s history and a lasting source of inspiration to scholars, journalists, students and future generations of communication professionals. The Faculty extended its heartfelt condolences to his family, colleagues, former students, the Association of Communication Scholars and Professionals of Nigeria (ACSPN), and the entire communication community. “We pray that God grants his loved ones the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss and that his remarkable legacy continues to illuminate the path for generations to come. May his soul rest in perfect peace.” The post UNILAG Faculty mourns Sobowale, celebrates legacy appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana explores centre of excellence for hearing, communication and cochlear implant care
items.description: Ghana is exploring the establishment of a Centre of Excellence for Hearing, Communication and Cochlear Implant Care to expand access to specialist hearing services and strengthen local healthcare capacity. The proposed centre would bring together services including hearing screening, diagnosis, ear, nose and throat (ENT) care, audiology, hearing technology, cochlear implant services, speech and language therapy, rehabilitation, family support and research. The proposal was discussed at a meeting involving Ambassador Victor Emmanuel Smith; Emilio Alonso Mendoza, president of the Alexander Graham Bell Association for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing (AG Bell); Roxana Semorile, president of Semorile Holdings, LLC; and Maabena Webb, executive director of Region17. Participants emphasised that the proposed centre should be Ghanaian-led and complement existing health and academic institutions rather than replace them. Ambassador Smith said the vision was to build an institution around Ghana’s healthcare priorities, infrastructure and professional workforce while strengthening services and expertise already available in the country. A key part of the proposal is to develop sustainable local expertise in hearing healthcare. Under the model discussed, international specialists would initially work alongside Ghanaian healthcare professionals to transfer skills and strengthen local capacity. Ghanaian professionals would subsequently be equipped to train others, helping to build a sustainable pipeline of expertise within the country. The initiative is also intended to position Ghana as a centre for professional training and knowledge-sharing, enabling local specialists to contribute to hearing healthcare across Africa. Hearing health remains an important public health concern, particularly for children, as early identification and appropriate intervention can influence language development, educational outcomes and future employment opportunities. The World Health Organization estimates that 4.8% of Ghana’s population lives with disabling hearing loss, according to figures cited in the proposal. The initiative is also aligned with the Ghana Health Service’s stated strategic direction for 2026 to 2036, which calls for equitable and integrated ear and hearing services across all 16 regions. Beyond providing treatment, the proposed centre is envisioned as a platform for professional training, research, innovation and regional knowledge exchange. Ambassador Smith expressed appreciation to participants for the discussions and indicated his interest in continued engagement to advance the proposal. The initiative’s guiding principle is to deliver care and train professionals in Ghana, retain knowledge locally and share Ghanaian expertise across Africa.

items.title: Firm eyes eyes Nigerian investment opportunities amid economic shifts
items.description: By Dickson Omobola Investment digital platform, Risevest, has said the Nigerian economy has undergone significant changes over the past two years, including exchange rate stabilisation, a decline in the benchmark interest rate and strong growth in the Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX. The firm, however, said the changing economy had made it necessary to evolve and provide Nigerians with greater exposure to investment opportunities. Risevest made this known at an event themed: ‘The Ascent,’ held in Lagos, where it announced plans to launch three mutual funds on its app and introduce Rise Business, a product designed to provide businesses with money management features. Speaking at the event, Risevest Product Manager, Ebube Ilo, said: “These changes require us to also evolve and give you greater exposure to more Nigerian opportunities, and that’s why today, for the first time, mutual funds are coming to Rise. We are launching three funds built around the three jobs that we believe your money should be doing: growth, liquidity, and income.” The Risevest Naira Equity Fund will be actively managed and invested in a basket of some of Nigeria’s strongest listed companies across six sectors: financial services, consumer goods, information and communications technology, oil and gas, industrial goods, and agriculture. The fund is designed to outperform the NGX 30. The Risevest Dollar Fund will comprise a professionally managed portfolio of dollar-denominated, low-risk investments, including Nigerian government eurobonds, corporate eurobonds and other money market instruments. The fund will not invest in equities. The Risevest Money Market Fund will invest in short-term, low-risk instruments such as treasury bills, fixed deposits, commercial papers and certificates of deposit. It is designed to keep investors’ money accessible while earning interest. Also speaking, Risevest Product Manager, Solomon Olalemi, said Rise Business was developed in response to a question the company had repeatedly received after more than five years of helping Nigerians hold and grow their money. “When can my business do the same?” he quoted business owners as asking. Rise Business will provide businesses with four accounts in their registered business names, denominated in US dollars, British pounds, euros and naira. Each account will have its own details that overseas clients and suppliers can verify. Businesses will also be able to send payments directly to recipients in more than 60 countries, receive money through their account numbers and convert between currencies, including the US dollar, British pound, euro, Canadian dollar and Chinese yuan, all from one platform. The product targets importers, exporters, small businesses, agencies and consultancies that regularly move money between Nigeria and other markets. The post Firm eyes eyes Nigerian investment opportunities amid economic shifts appeared first on Vanguard News .
